Methodology

Source: vignettes/articles/methodology.Rmd
methodology.Rmd

This article documents where howbig’s numbers come from: the simulated networks, how each method is scored, how the grid is used, and how the answers were checked.

Simulated networks

Each simulated design starts from two networks: group 1, and group 2, which equals group 1 plus a localized change.

Group 1 is built in four steps:

  1. Blocks. Features are split into blocks of 25 (designs with p < 50 use two equal blocks). Each block is a Barabási-Albert preferential-attachment graph.
  2. Between-block edges. Pairs in different blocks connect with probability 0.01 × 5 / B for B blocks, which keeps the expected number of between-block edges roughly constant as p grows.
  3. Edge weights. Weights are drawn from an empirical, metabolomics-derived distribution of partial correlations, excluding |weight| < 0.035.
  4. Precision matrix. Each off-diagonal entry is divided by 1.5 times its row’s absolute sum (Danaher et al. 2014), the diagonal is set to 1, and the diagonal is boosted if needed to make the matrix positive definite.

Group 2 applies one of three perturbations:

perturbation What changes Setting in the source study
"structural" All edges within block 1 are deleted A
"magnitude" Off-diagonal precision entries in block 1 are scaled by 1.5; no edges appear or disappear C
"both" Block 1 deleted and block 2 scaled by 1.5 B

Scaling is applied after the precision matrix is built, so the row-sum normalization cannot cancel it.

Ground truth. An edge is differential when the two groups’ precision entries differ by more than 0.01, i.e. |Θ₁ − Θ₂| > 0.01. This definition counts strength changes as well as edges that appear or disappear.

Data. Each group’s samples are drawn from a zero-mean multivariate normal with that group’s covariance (the inverse precision).

Differential edges are rare, and rarer as p grows

Because the change is confined to one or two blocks, the share of feature pairs that are truly differential falls sharply with p. That is the main reason designs with many features need large samples. Computed with the package’s own generator:

Features (p) Feature pairs Differential pairs (mean) Share differential
50 1225 40 3.27%
100 4950 46 0.93%
250 31125 52 0.17%
500 124750 51 0.04%

Methods

Each method runs with the same fixed configuration it had in the simulation study:

Method Package Configuration Edge score for ranking
JGL_BIC JGL Fused penalty; λ₁ then λ₂ chosen by BIC over a data-adaptive 10-value grid |Θ̂₁ − Θ̂₂|
JGL_BIC_GGL JGL Group penalty; same tuning |Θ̂₁ − Θ̂₂|
SSJGL spikeyglass Fused spike-and-slab; 3-step v₀ ladder |Θ̂₁ − Θ̂₂|
SSJGL_GGL spikeyglass Group spike-and-slab; same ladder |Θ̂₁ − Θ̂₂|
multiGGM multiGGM SSVS; 2 chains × (5,000 burn-in + 1,000 saved) |Θ̂₁ − Θ̂₂| masked to edges with posterior inclusion ≥ 0.05
JRF iJRFNet 1,000 trees, mtry = √(p − 1) |importance₁ − importance₂|
InvCov (base R) Inverse sample covariance (pseudoinverse when singular) |Θ̂₁ − Θ̂₂|

Scoring

FDR-controlled calls. Power needs a set of edges each method declares differential at the FDR target:

  • Frequentist methods are compared to a permutation null. One representative network pair is generated. For each of n_perm permutations, fresh data are drawn, group labels are shuffled, and the method is refit. The edge scores from all permutations are pooled into one null distribution. Each observed edge score gets an empirical p-value against the pooled null, and the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure is applied at the target.
  • multiGGM (Bayesian) uses its posterior probabilities directly. Edges are ranked by their posterior probability of differing, and the largest top set whose average (1 − probability) stays at or below the target is declared.

From those calls:

  • Sensitivity (power) = true differential edges declared / all true differential edges.
  • Achieved FDR = declared edges that are not truly differential / all declared edges.
  • AUPR, a threshold-free secondary measure: area under the precision-recall curve of the edge ranking.

Each replicate draws a fresh network and data. The reported value is the mean over replicates, with the 10th-90th percentile band showing how much power varies between networks.

The grid

The precomputed grid holds two one-dimensional sweeps (100 replicates per cell for most cells) that cross at one anchor:

  • sample-size arm: n = 250, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000 at p = 250;
  • feature arm: p = 50, 100, 200, 250, 300, 500 at n = 1000;
  • perturbation: structural, magnitude, and both at the anchor (p = 250, n = 1000), plus one off-arm cell (p = 125, n = 100).

Some cells lack a scored sensitivity (for example, JGL and SSJGL at p = 500, where permutation nulls were not computed); there howbig reports AUPR and suggests simulating. One cell (JRF at p = 250, n = 2000) has only 2 replicates, and howbig flags it.

Interpolation

Queries on an arm, between grid points, are interpolated with a monotone (Fritsch-Carlson) spline on log(n) or log(p). Interpolation never extrapolates past the ends of an arm, and never crosses between arms.

That restriction is deliberate and was tested:

Check Result
Leave-one-out along the feature arm (AUPR) mean absolute error 0.007
Leave-one-out along the sample-size arm (AUPR) 0.03 overall; JRF up to 0.20 (its curve bends sharply)
Predicting the off-arm cell (p = 125, n = 100) by combining the two arms errors around 0.20, consistently too optimistic
Interpolated vs freshly simulated, p = 150, n = 1000, JGL_BIC sensitivity 0.65 vs 0.65 (± 0.02)

So on-arm interpolation is trustworthy, while combining arms to predict off-arm designs is not; howbig simulates those instead.

On-demand simulation

simulate_power() runs the pipeline above for any design, with the same network family as the shipped grid, so grid and simulated answers describe the same networks. It was checked by re-simulating grid cells:

Design Grid Simulated (20 replicates)
InvCov, p = 100, n = 1000 0.49 0.48
JGL_BIC, p = 100, n = 1000 0.70 0.68 (± 0.02)

Implementation notes:

  • Reproducible. Every replicate and permutation sets its own seed from seed, so results are identical however many cores are used.
  • Parallel-safe. Workers are separate R processes rather than forks. Forking after a multithreaded linear-algebra library (such as Apple Accelerate) has started can crash the workers.
  • Runtime estimates come from a per-method regression of log fit time on log(p) and log(n), fit to the production timings. It predicts within about 30%.

Source

The simulation design, generators, and scoring are ported from the simulation study for the DiNA differential network analysis tutorial (manuscript in preparation). The shipped grid is the study’s interim Barabási-Albert tree family (mean degree ~1.9); it will be replaced by the scale-free family (mean degree ~3.8), matching the networks of Danaher et al. (2014).

Danaher, P., Wang, P., & Witten, D. M. (2014). The joint graphical lasso for inverse covariance estimation across multiple classes. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 76(2), 373-397.
